title: Every time Diddy changed his name, he washed away another batch of old scandals
dek: Each of Sean Combs's renamings over thirty years was a brand reboot: control the room, control the guest list, control the narrative, and clear out the old scandals one by one — until Cassie Ventura's lawsuit finally couldn't be covered up.
why: This is not a celebrity-fall retelling. It takes apart a liability-shielding machine that ran for thirty years: who stayed silent, who benefited, and why even the reporter herself has to ask whether she was complicit.
who: Readers, journalists and researchers interested in how celebrity power operates; especially for anyone trying to understand why, when "everyone knew," no one spoke.
skip: After 42:02 it's a review of a different film, unrelated to this episode — you can skip it.

points.h: Pop culture had been telling this as a joke for decades
points.body: More than twenty years before Combs was taken into custody, pop culture was already making jokes about his parties and his temper. The host plays two clips: in the 2000 film Scary Movie, Regina Hall's Brenda describes how Puff Daddy's pool parties get out of control; in a 2008 Mad TV parody of Hannah Montana, P. Diddy films everything on a camera phone. There were earlier warning signs too: a record label executive blacklisted him over how he treated women, someone at Howard said they had seen him beat a woman with a belt outside his girlfriend's dorm, and on tour his entourage left behind a stolen handgun. Roundtree's judgment is that this was almost background noise in the industry — it was just that his spectacle was bigger than every incident that surfaced along the timeline, and it covered all the allegations.

points.h: He was the gatekeeper of New York culture
points.body: Roundtree says that in that period he was simply the gatekeeper of culture in New York. The people who wanted in weren't only music people; they were power brokers, models, actors. He controlled who got in and controlled the atmosphere of the room, so everyone had to court him. She points out in particular that this network was cashable: being able to control the environment and make people curry favour for entry meant he later turned those connections into business deals, and into that identity of "everyone wants to be around him." Early on, all of it was dressed up as "relax, hang out with people in the industry"; only later did the civil suits reclassify it — the plaintiffs say those occasions were where they were sexually assaulted.

points.h: His success itself was his shield
points.body: Mosley runs through his 2000s empire — records, clothing, vodka, restaurants, television and film — and notes he fits the same pattern as Trump, whom he publicly admired: after every scandal he didn't just survive, he got bigger. Roundtree dates the starting point to the City College incident: a charity basketball game he helped promote, raising money for HIV/AIDS, was oversold, a stampede broke out, and nine people died. The investigation found him partly responsible for inadequate security, he paid a large settlement to the victims' families, but reputationally and professionally it was "business as usual." She says his success protected him all along — first Uptown Records covered for him because he had already proven his value, and later so did Mary J. Blige's success.

points.h: Nine albums signed, one album released
points.body: Cassie signed to Bad Boy at 19 and was with Combs for nearly 11 years. Roundtree says the relationship was unconventional: the two never lived together, and she was never included in his family holidays, which was itself a major point of friction between them. She released only one album but was signed for nine more. Sources told Roundtree that Cassie was always making music and always wanted to continue her own music career, but Combs would deliberately stall singles and albums, using power over her career as a weapon — when they fought he would say, "Your show is cancelled. You're not getting your album. This isn't coming out." After a demo that was supposed to be her follow-up album leaked, The Guardian's review said it would have been album of the year.

points.h: The jury believed the abuse, not the coercion
points.body: The prosecution's core theory was that these hotel sex occasions constituted sex trafficking because the women were coerced into taking part. For Cassie, they argued physical violence was the coercive means of keeping her compliant; for the woman known as Jane, they argued the financial support itself was the coercion. Roundtree thinks coercion is extremely hard to prove. After the verdict a juror came out to explain, and at least one said she believed Cassie's account of domestic abuse but couldn't prove his intent to coerce them, and that's where the charge stalled. The way Jane entered the case is telling too: she never filed a civil suit; the prosecution found her messages in Combs's texts three days after Cassie sued, and she wrote that it felt like reading her own sexual trauma — and she had previously been cooperating with Combs's defence lawyers.

points.h: This is also a workplace story
points.body: Roundtree repeatedly stresses that the prosecution never made this clear: it is also a workplace story, and nearly every major witness had worked for Combs. As employees they were forced to witness domestic abuse, felt threatened themselves, and feared being blacklisted by the industry if they spoke. Strip away the lurid shell and it was an environment that pushed employees into a personal-assistant role serving the boss's sex life — supplying drugs, cleaning up humiliating hotel rooms, covering up his domestic abuse of his girlfriend. Their ambitions were to make music and learn the industry, and their lives revolved around this instead. People who tried to report it or leave were fired, thrown out; one says she was pinned on a car hood, pushed out a door, her arm slammed into a wall. She says it was these consequences that created a culture of silence.

The government called it a criminal enterprise, but only Combs was charged. His defence lawyer asked in return: if there was a conspiracy, where are the co-conspirators? Roundtree says the absence of co-conspirators testifying is the prosecution's biggest hole. When you hear "conspiracy," "organized racketeering," what comes to mind is the mob, a big organization with big guns; and when the picture is drawn as one man, his assistant, his old bodyguard friend he grew up with, plus a few fresh college graduates as the co-conspirators, it's hard to line up the concept of "organized racketeering" with "that's them?" Separately, more than twenty men have also accused Combs of sexual misconduct or assault, but their experiences barely entered the criminal case — Roundtree says that didn't fit the prosecution's working theory.

points.h: The comeback script is already being written
points.body: Combs is expected to be released in early 2028. Roundtree mentions a Netflix documentary produced by 50 Cent that recently won an editing Emmy; it includes real-time footage of him before his September 2024 arrest, planning his own documentary and comeback story. She says this confirms once again that he has always kept tight control of his image, and we should expect the same after his release. There have also been recent reports that he is in touch with someone who does digital communications so he can keep track of what social media says about him at any moment. Roundtree has no doubt that once out, he will tell these years his own way.
